title: The US Government Is Considering Shutting Down International Flights at Every Major Airport Indian Americans Use
excerpt: DHS Secretary names SFO, JFK, Newark, LAX, O'Hare, and Seattle as possible targets. The plan would halt customs and immigration processing at 'sanctuary city' airports — weeks before the FIFA World Cup.
body:
The Department of Homeland Security is drawing up plans to stop processing international travelers and cargo at major U.S. airports in so-called "sanctuary cities" — municipalities that have declined to cooperate with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. If implemented, the move would effectively shut down international air travel at the airports most heavily used by Indian Americans.

The Airports on the List

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin named eight airports in a Fox News interview on Tuesday: Denver, Philadelphia, Chicago O'Hare, Los Angeles International, JFK and Newark in the New York area, Seattle-Tacoma, and San Francisco International. No decision has been made, Mullin emphasized, but the fact that names are being spoken aloud on cable television means the planning has moved beyond the theoretical.

These are not fringe airports. They are the backbone of international connectivity for the United States. Combined, they handle the vast majority of nonstop flights to India — SFO, Newark, and JFK alone account for nearly every direct Air India, United, and American Airlines route between the two countries.

What It Would Mean for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.8 million Indian Americans in the United States, these airports are not optional. They are the gateway home. SFO serves the Bay Area's enormous tech workforce. Newark and JFK are the primary hubs for the East Coast's Indian population stretching from New Jersey to Connecticut. O'Hare connects the Midwest. LAX serves Southern California's growing diaspora.

If customs and immigration processing were halted at these airports, international travelers — including U.S. citizens returning from abroad — would have no way to clear federal inspection. Airlines would be unable to operate inbound international flights. The ripple effects would cascade through the travel industry within days.

The FIFA World Cup Complication

The timing makes the proposal even more explosive. The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off across the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June. Millions of international visitors are expected, and several host cities — including Los Angeles, Seattle, and the New York metro area — are on Mullin's list.

The travel industry has already raised alarms. Halting international processing at these airports would not just inconvenience travelers; it would strand them. Airlines would be forced to reroute or cancel flights, hotels would lose bookings, and the economic damage would run into the billions.

The Political Context

The proposal is the latest escalation in a years-long standoff between the federal government and Democratic-led cities over immigration enforcement. Sanctuary cities limit their cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, refusing to hold detained immigrants beyond their release dates or share certain information with federal agents.

The Trump administration has framed this as obstruction. Critics argue that weaponizing airport processing — a federal function — to punish local governments would harm millions of people who have nothing to do with immigration policy, including American citizens, legal permanent residents, and H-1B visa holders.

What Happens Next

Mullin said he had met with White House officials but stressed that no final decision had been made. The plan remains under consideration. But the mere discussion has already rattled the travel industry, and for Indian Americans who depend on these airports for everything from business travel to family visits, the uncertainty alone is a disruption.

The airports named are not obscure regional hubs. They are the connective tissue of American international travel. If the federal government follows through, it will be the most dramatic use of immigration enforcement power against American cities in modern history — and the Indian diaspora will be among the first to feel it.
author: Diaspora Desk
